technology.title: AWS adds virtual iPhones to its cloud
technology.description: AWS now offers two new types of cloudy computers: emulated Androids and simulated iPhones. The cloudy colossus announced both virtual offerings on Wednesday. They’re part of its Device Farm service, which previously saw AWS offer developers the chance to test their software on actual iOS and Android devices that reside in the Amazonian cloud. AWS will now also host virtual devices running Android and iOS. AWS touts the virtual mobile devices as superior to physical devices. “With virtual devices, you can shift testing left to stages that need high speed and volume, such as pull requests, code merges, and smoke tests, and keep real devices for later stages that need high fidelity, such as regression and release testing,” the cloudy business unit argues in its launch announcement. AWS also says developers can get to work faster on a virtual iPhone or Pixel. “Virtual devices running the latest device and OS typically start in seconds, and others start in around a minute,” the outfit argues. That may sound appetizing, but Amazon’s menu of virtual devices is short and bland. When The Register logged on as an AWS user, the only emulated Android phone listed was a Google Pixel 10, running Android 15, 16, or 17. An emulated Pixel tablet running Android 17 is also on the menu. At the time of writing, we could find only a virtual iPhone 16, running iOS 18.6, 23.61, and 27.0. Analyst firm Counterpoint’s list of the world’s top 10 best-selling smartphones in Q2 of 2026 does not include a single Pixel device. The iPhone 16 occupies 10 th place. iPhone 17 models occupy the first, second, third, and seventh place on the list. AWS might excite more developers if it adds emulators for the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, Galaxy A07 4G, A17 5G, A17 4G, and Galaxy S26, as they occupy the fourth, fifth, sixth, eighth and ninth places on Counterpoint’s list. Amazon’s choice of a Pixel tablet is also an oddity given analyst firm IDC doesn’t list Google among its top five tablet vendors . Amazon does offer physical Galaxy A17 devices and three versions of the iPhone 17. But Device Farm doesn’t offer any foldable devices, meaning developers struggling to wrap their heads around the iPhone Duo will need either ask Apple for a loaner or shell out $2,000 to acquire one. At least developers don’t have to change behavior to access the few virtual devices AWS offers, as existing Device Farm APIs and test frameworks will work on real or notional machines. ®

technology.title: Free e-government platform that serves two billion people in ten countries has critical SQL injection bug
technology.description: India’s free e-government platform has a critical SQL injection flaw that thousands of organizations must patch to protect up to two billion citizens. The platform is called the Digital Infrastructure for Governance (Impact and Transformation) – aka DIGIT – and is a modular suite that offers common services such as authentication and payment collection. Third party developers can also create DIGIT modules, and plenty have done so and now offer add-ons that handle tasks as diverse as managing birth and death certificates, revenue collection, and running water treatment plants. DIGIT is ubiquitous in India, where all state and union territory governments use the platform, as do over 20,000 local government entities. India also exports DIGIT under its policy of turning software created for its own needs into “digital public goods” (DPI) that it happily gives away to other nations. Nine nations have implemented DIGIT to some degree, among them Mozambique, Liberia, Senegal, Nigeria, Burundi, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Jamaica, and Sri Lanka India’s population is 1.4 billion. Indonesia’s is 280 million and Nigeria is home to 240 million. DIGIT is therefore used by governments that serve over two billion people, some of whom are now at risk thanks to CVE-2026-136706 , a 9.3-rated SQL injection flaw present in DIGIT which allows “improper neutralization of user supplied input while constructing SQL queries and execution in the affected User and Access Control Service components.” “An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending specially crafted input through the affected API endpoint to the targeted system,” according to CERT-IN . “Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary SQL queries, potentially resulting in unauthorized disclosure, modification or deletion of database information on the targeted system.” eGov India, which oversees work on DIGIT, has released source code for an update that fixes the problem. While local government users of DIGIT typically access it as SaaS, through large implementations run by national or state governments, over 1,000 deployments are live across various cities and other entities. Those orgs can therefore add patching DIGIT to their urgent to-do lists, along with fixing Java , PHP , vCenter and any other widely used technologies that suddenly need an urgent security update. ®

technology.title: The token factory never sleeps
technology.description: Agentic AI has supercharged demand for inference infrastructure. According to Goldman Sachs, token consumption is set to jump 24-fold to 120 quadrillion tokens per month between this year and 2030. Enterprises, wary of frontier model sticker shock, are now building their own GPU estates to cope. Those enterprises shouldn't blindly follow hyperscalers' lead when taking AI inference kit into production. The indicators of success for such companies are different than those for a frontier model provider, and so are the constraints. DIY AI infrastructure at the enterprise level has to earn ROI quickly, meaning that enterprises must focus on sustained operation. That makes engineering criteria such as uptime, heat and power, service windows, and deployment times doubly important. The performance benchmarks that hyperscalers focus on won't matter nearly as much to the average bank or retailer. ASUS is presenting the ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System , built on the NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 platform, as a worked example of sustained AI inference infrastructure. It announced two models at NVIDIA GTC Berlin in October: the 3U hybrid-cooled XR R1I12B-M1BHFS and the 2U fully liquid-cooled XR R1I12B-M1BLFS . Agents change the compute bill Agents represent a hockey stick curve for token consumption because an agent isn't a single prompt. It loops until the job's done, often spawning other versions of itself in the process. This is how it breaks a goal into steps and works through them iteratively. While training is a batch workload, agent inference is a production service that runs around the clock and only gets bigger. NVIDIA is making each generation of systems more powerful than the last to keep up with the demands of both. Running at scale, day after day, is another matter. A useful way to think about the infrastructure that does it is as a token factory: it takes in power, data and GPU compute and turns out tokens. What counts is throughput, meaning how many tokens, and how many users, the same power and floor space can serve, hour after hour. Enterprises move from pilots to AI factories Enterprises are moving ahead quickly with their AI factory projects. According to Deloitte's AI infrastructure survey , published in March, 64 percent of respondents have started limited or at-scale AI factory deployments, while 88 percent expect to do so by 2028. They are spending more on AI infrastructure to do it: 86 percent expect their budgets to increase over the next three years. Enterprises have different problems from hyperscalers and frontier model companies, though. Model builders often get to design greenfield campuses around their GPUs. Conversely, enterprises are often working with small operations teams in existing datacenters that may not have been built with AI in mind. technology.title: Microsoft: Hackers in China, N Korea using ARTEX AI tool to break into global tech systems
technology.description: Chinese and North Korean state-sponsored hacking crews are among the growing number of groups known for using the ARTEX pentesting tool in attacks, Microsoft said this week. ARTEX is an open source, AI-powered penetration testing framework that attackers have adopted to automate reconnaissance, credential attacks, and exploitation since its public release in July. Campaigns that have been linked to ARTEX have targeted cloud environments, IT software like ConnectWise , and financial institutions globally, sometimes reaching privileged access in under three hours. Salt Typhoon is arguably the most recognizable name on the list of ARTEX beneficiaries – the group responsible for attacks on telcos AT&T and Verizon , US government systems , UK prime minister's aides , and more. The lesser-known Crystal Typhoon – the group behind the ArcaneDoor attacks back when Microsoft called it Storm-1849 – was also named alongside it, as were North Korea's Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet. Microsoft also named China-state-aligned Storm-0940, linked to the ConnectWise compromise, and financially motivated, Cambodia-based Storm-3358. It had previously reported both groups' use of ARTEX. Chinese cybersecurity company ThreatBook claimed ownership of ARTEX in November. GitHub user "Autumn-27" originally published its source code with a Chinese-language interface in July. Various forks of the repo, which was taken down in October, have meant that the same framework is available in multiple languages. According to Infrawatch , there are more than 130 variants of ARTEX in circulation, and it is the most widely used agentic offensive framework (AOF) at present. Like other offensive security tools adopted by criminals, ARTEX can lower the effort required to mount attacks. Experienced groups can also use it to automate repetitive work and pursue multiple avenues at once. As Microsoft echoed this week, after the FBI and AWS issued their warnings earlier this month , ARTEX is proving to be a useful tool for the more sophisticated groups to streamline and hasten their attacks too. It's being used to help attackers steal AI and cloud credentials at "industrial scale," as AWS put it, which provide attackers access to advanced models for free. Microsoft says ARTEX can progress from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access within minutes, depending on its configuration and the target's defenses. "In the past few weeks, we've reported several distinct campaigns that abused ARTEX to search public repositories for exposed secrets, enable supply chain compromise, and scan internet-facing systems for exploitation," its threat intelligence team blogged . "These campaigns illustrate how threat actors use ARTEX to automate various stages of the attack chain. technology.title: Tech's outage problem needs maintenance, not conspiracy theories
technology.description: Years of technical debt, increasingly complex systems, and underinvestment in IT operations have left organizations vulnerable to major outages, according to Forrester. The analyst pointed to a seven-day stretch in November when failures disrupted Microsoft 365, US air traffic control, banking, and other critical services. The coinciding outages provoked "a slew of conspiracy theories about cyberattacks and AI," Forrester said. "The real culprit is tragically mundane: the culmination of decades of technical debt, the frenetic buildout of massively complex and highly interdependent systems, the concentration of risk, and the underinvestment in advanced operations." Forrester urged technology suppliers and in-house IT teams to prioritize resilience as their systems grow more complex. Otherwise, "the tech estate will collapse like a house of cards, taking down consumer and business trust with it." Earlier this month, Microsoft was left struggling to restore many of its cloud services after a core process running on some servers became "overwhelmed" and its attempts to fix the problem failed. Some of its services did not recover for another 24 hours. In October, Google Cloud blamed a "power event" for taking down multiple online products for customers in Western Europe. Affected services included BigQuery Data Transfer Service, Cloud Filestore, Cloud Run, Google App Engine, and Google Kubernetes Engine. In October last year , a major outage impacted Amazon Web Services (AWS), with even Amazon's own web page reported to be offline and dozens of other online services and websites affected. Aviation and banking were also hit this month. A communications outage triggered a nationwide ground stop in the US on November 13 , while incidents involving JPMorgan Chase, United Airlines, Apple, Workday, Gmail, and other services added to the sense of widespread instability. "Claims that these were all part of one connected cyberattack or conspiracy are highly unlikely. The real story is much more mundane," the report said . Forrester argued that organizations have prioritized visible improvements over repairs to the underlying technology. "Modernization investments have favored visible change over structural renewal," wrote report authors Lauren Nelson and Mark Moccia. "Organizations routinely fund new customer experiences, cloud migrations, platform consolidation, and AI initiatives because leaders can connect them to growth or productivity. "They are less enthusiastic about updating core systems, simplifying architectures, retiring obsolete components, and eliminating fragile interfaces. The result is a modern front end resting on an aging, brittle, and increasingly interconnected estate." Forrester's recommendations are to map dependencies, test failures and recovery under realistic conditions, and use incidents and near misses to identify weaknesses before they cause another outage. ®

technology.title: UK privacy watchdog faces probe into its workplace culture
technology.description: Britain's privacy watchdog is getting a taste of its own medicine, with an independent review set to examine the culture, governance, and accountability surrounding the events that led to former Information Commissioner John Edwards' resignation. Karon Monaghan KC will examine whether the regulator's culture and governance allowed problems to develop or made concerns harder to raise. Edwards quit in June after an independent workplace investigation found there was a "case to answer" over his behavior and that his conduct fell short of what was expected of a public official. He disagreed with some of its findings, but ultimately conceded that he had shown "poor judgment." That investigation, however, focused on Edwards alone. According to the terms of reference published on Thursday, it "did not consider the wider conditions in which that conduct occurred, and it was not designed to." The new review will cast a wider net. Monaghan wants to know whether staff could call out bad behavior further up the food chain, and what awaited those who tried. It will also poke around the regulator's leadership and governance arrangements and its relationship with its sponsoring government department, including whether there were adequate ways for concerns to be escalated and those at the top to be challenged. Current and former staff can give evidence confidentially and voluntarily, while Monaghan will be given access to relevant documents and existing material, including staff surveys and data on bullying, harassment and discrimination. The ICO has confirmed it won't use confidentiality clauses in settlement agreements to prevent people from contributing to the review. Monaghan decides which witnesses and documents are relevant, rather than the ICO or DCMS. Access remains subject to legal restrictions, and she must be told when material is withheld and why. She can speak to whoever she thinks is relevant and ask for the complaints, correspondence, and other paperwork she needs. And if that leads her somewhere unexpected, she can ask to widen the investigation. DCMS can refuse, but it won't be able to quietly brush the request aside, and any decision not to expand the scope has to make it into the final report. The review won't reopen the investigation into Edwards, make findings about the conduct of named individuals, or delve into the merits of the regulator's enforcement decisions. Its arrival comes amid a broader shake-up at Britain's data watchdog. The old Information Commissioner's Office was formally replaced by the Information Commission on September 30, bringing with it a new board-led governance model. The government first promised the wider review in July, shortly after Edwards' departure, but it didn't appoint its reviewer or nail down the terms until late November. science.title: Astronomers watch a red giant star greedily devour a stellar 'Bao bun' before erupting: 'We couldn't quite believe our luck'
science.description: null Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star. That isn't a random comparison. The cannibal star, which is 350 times bigger than the sun, is nicknamed "Big Bao," while its unfortunate companion had the nickname "Little Bao." The cute cosmic monikers come from the fact that this destructive merger event has been designated AT2025abao. A Bao bun might be a little snack for a human, but this red giant star made a real meal out of Little Bao. This cannibalistic event was tracked by a wide array of ground- and space-based telescopes, including NASA space missions NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), as well as the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii. The conclusion of the event AT2025abao was marked by a massive eruption witnessed in Oct. 2025 by two instruments at Caltech's Palomar Observatory: the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the Wide-field INfrared Transient ExploreR (WINTER). "The excitement was real," team member Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "We couldn't quite believe our luck. With detailed observations for several years before the merger, for the first time, we now have an unprecedented glimpse of the conditions that lead to such cosmic events." Reconstructing a violent cosmic collision The story of AT2025abao began when astronomers detected a bright flash in the nearby Andromeda galaxy , a region where scientists hadn't expected to see a cosmic explosion. Responding to this unexpected flash, Karambelkar and colleagues set about investigating its cause with a plethora of telescopes. This led to them seeing a slow and continuous brightening over the course of two years, They determined the cause of the flash was a rare stellar merger, the luminous red nova now designated AT2025abao. They linked this to a star called WNTR23bzdiq / WTP19aalzlk that had been observed steadily brightening since 2019 after being stable for the preceding 30 years. Thus, the team determined that at the heart of the event is a red giant, a star that puffs out to hundreds of times its original size after it runs out of hydrogen in its core. The team theorizes that Big Bao, with a mass seven times greater than the sun, expanded so rapidly and violently that it swallowed its smaller companion star. The unfortunate star, Little Bao, then spiraled into Big Bao's core in fewer than 10 orbits. "A couple of years back, we discovered a star that was gradually brightening. We took a closer look to discover a red giant, or a star that has started to expand toward the end of its life, just like our sun will one day," Karambelkar said. "Steady brightening was unusual, but even if something was stirring, no one expected to see an explosion in their lifetime, as these stars remain relatively stable for thousands of years." science.title: New Scientist Book Club: How urine changed the course of human history
science.description: A detail from Joseph Wright’s 1771 painting The Alchemist Discovering Phosphorus, showing Henning Brand in 1669 Science History Images/Alamy Imagine you could boil the development of science down to a single ingredient. A magical, mystical compound that transformed human history. Of course, science doesn’t work that way; even if breakthroughs shift the paradigm of our understanding, discovery doesn’t progress like a tech tree in a computer game, but as an interweaving tapestry of complementary and competing ideas and experimentation. Theories can bubble under the surface for centuries, overlooked because of politics or failure to realise their implications, while innovations can emerge from taking an idea in one industry and transplanting it to another. But, for a moment, try and picture what just one such ingredient could be. What would you pick? For centuries, in medieval Europe, alchemists quested for the “Philosopher’s Stone” that would finally help them achieve their dreams of transmutation. It was a search doomed to failure from the very beginning. And yet, a far better idea was under their noses – or, rather, their underpants – the entire time. My pick? Urine has a strong case for being the most transformative substance in human history. Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter The development of civilisation was built on chemistry. It required the first chemical reaction we mastered – fire – to keep us warm, cook our food and smelt ores. But leatherwork played an equally key role. Urine is a source of urea, which bacteria can break down into ammonia, granting early humans easy access to a base that could soften organic matter and tan hides. Across the world, leatherwork became the cornerstone of survival for every civilisation, from the Americas to Europe, Africa and Asia: even cultures that didn’t develop a bronze age, such as the Aztec, or skipped it entirely, as seen in Sub-Saharan Africa, relied on leatherwork for clothes, structures, industry and commerce. Advertisement If the power of pee helped build civilisation, it would go on to be foundational in its upkeep. In ancient Rome, urine was so useful for laundries to keep togas whiter-than-white that Emperor Vespasian levied a tax on draining urinals. When his son complained, Vespasian’s response was blunt: pecunia non olet , money doesn’t stink. Part of the funds were used to build the Colosseum in Rome, today recognised as one of the wonders of the world. The magic of urine filtered into what would become chemical science, too. In the Leiden Papyrus X , part of a cluster of the only original manuscripts on alchemy’s origins we still have, you can find a recipe for faking gold using polysulfides. At first, the raider was frustrated; scavenging the tombs near Thebes, he had hoped to uncover a priceless heirloom, or a nugget of gold that would sparkle with lustre in the starlight. Instead, he had found only a clutch of rolled scrolls, made of papyrus and sealed against the elements. For a moment, he considered casting the documents aside and leaving them for the desert. Then greed got the better of him. Westerners loved all things Egyptian, he reasoned. Since the French had arrived with Napoleon, the new field of “Egyptology” had swept the continent, capturing the imagination of scholars and the wealthy. It was almost as popular as the new science of “chemistry”. Surely, if he took his find to the market, he’d find some gullible fool willing to buy it. The buyer’s name was Jean d’Anastasy, and he was anything but a fool. Born in Greece as the son of a Damascus merchant who had won and lost his fortune in the Napoleonic Wars, d’Anastasy had used his family’s connections to set himself up as a grain merchant in Alexandria, before scheming his way into being named the local Consul General for Sweden and Norway. science.title: Shivelyuch Socked In
science.description: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Shivelyuch Socked In Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search In the same way that Shivelyuch (also called Shiveluch) frequently displays volcanic activity, it is also chronically obscured by clouds. When the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured this image on November 8, 2026, clouds encroached on the snowy mountain on Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula . But they hovered beneath the volcano’s 3,283-meter (10,771-foot) peak, leaving a clear opening over its caldera and northern upper slopes. The upper reaches of Shivelyuch feature a caldera 9 kilometers (5.6 miles) wide that is open to the south. A lava dome , formed by vents extruding viscous magma, appears as a dark area within it. Lava domes on Shivelyuch go through cycles of growth and collapse, with collapses sometimes setting off fast-moving avalanches of hot ash and rock called pyroclastic flows . In November 2026, effusive eruptions of lava and explosive activity at Shivelyuch had been ongoing for months , according to reports from the Kamchatka Volcanic Eruption Response Team (KVERT). science.description: null Venus is at its most dazzling in the predawn sky this week as it shines close to the bright star Spica in the southeast. Here's what you need to know. As an inner planet, Venus never strays far from the horizon, at least compared to outer planets like Jupiter and Mars which can be visible all night long during opposition, when they shine opposite the sun in Earth's sky. Instead, Venus alternates between morning and evening appearances. All the while, its shifting moon-like phases and ever-changing proximity to Earth causes its brightness to wax and wane. When is Venus at its most dazzling? Venus will reach peak brightness during its current morning apparition at 1:37 p.m. EST (1837 GMT) on Nov. 27 according to the astronomy website In-The-Sky . Spica is a double system of two stars that orbit one another once every four days. Its stars are separated by just approximately 11 million miles (less than 18 million kilometers), making them far too close to split visually with even the most powerful amateur equipment. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 26, 2011: NASA's 2-ton nuclear-powered Curiosity rover launches to Mars
science.description: null On November 26, 2011, the NASA Curiosity rover launched to Mars. The Mars rover Curiosity was the biggest and most powerful rover anyone had ever sent to the Red Planet. The 2-ton science laboratory is about the size of a small SUV. The mission's goal was to search for habitable environments on Mars , or evidence that the planet could have been habitable in the past. It launched on an Atlas V rocket from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida. About nine months later, Curiosity made a challenging landing on Mars. It successfully used a new landing technology called a sky crane to gently lower it to the surface. NASA's Curiosity rover lifts off atop a United Launch Alliance Atlas V rocket on Nov. 26, 2011 from Florida's Cape Canaveral Air Force Station. (Image credit: collectSPACE/Robert Z. Pearlman ) Why it mattered It may be hard to imagine now, but 15 years ago, the idea of a nuclear-powered rover on Mars was just a concept. When the Curiosity rover launched in 2011, it made that idea a reality the car-size probe (using a plutonium-based radioisotope thermoelectric generator that converts heat from radioactive decay into power) as it headed to the Red Planet. Curiosity was the largest rover ever launched to Mars, following up on the success of the tiny Sojourner rover in 1997 and the larger twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity in 2004. Its sky crane landing system was novel at the time, and fully automated. Once it began its descent in August 2012, NASA could only wait through "seven minutes of terror" to see how it turned out. It ended being a huge success. NASA's Curiosity rover on Mars. (Image credit: NASA) After its smooth landing, Curiosity lived up to its original name: the Mars Science Laboratory. Within weeks, Curiosity fulfilled its primary mission. It found evidence of ancient running water on Mars . It later found organic molecules on Mars as well. Curiosity's primary mission was expected to last just about one Martian year (687 Earth days, or about two Earth years), as the rover explored its Gale Crater landing site. But NASA has extended the mission as the rover continues to operate in good health. In fact, Curiosity has survived long enough to welcome its successor to Mars, the Perseverance rover , which landed in February 2021 on a mission to collect the first samples for later retrieval. Perseverance used the same basic 2-ton design, plutonium power system and sky crane landing system to reach Mars. And today, a ground-based twin of the Curiosity rover, called Promise , is being outfitted for an upcoming mission to the moon. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

science.title: Cosmic 'betta fish' glows in spectacular nebula portrait | Space photo of the day for Nov. 26, 2026
science.description: null An image captured by the Dark Energy Camera showcasing the Betta Fish Nebula. (Image credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA) The striking blue of the Betta Fish Nebula swims across the cosmic landscape, a stunning wisp of material leftover from a stellar explosion. What is it? Roughly 6,800 light-years from Earth and nestled in the Centaurus constellation, this piece of the supernova remnant SNR G295.5+09.7 has earned the nickname the Betta Fish Nebula for its floaty, fishy shape. This almost ghostly whirl of gas and dust was created when a star much more massive than our sun exploded, blasting its outer layers of material outward in the process. Over time, the remnants of this supernova eruption stretched outward into space, dispersing and colliding with surrounding gas. The explosive remnants mixing with gas in the interstellar medium created this glowing, blue cloud. This celestial scene was captured by the Dark Energy Camera (DECam), that was created by the U.S. Department of Energy. The camera is installed on the National Science Foundation's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile. Why is it incredible? This image of a colossal, cosmic "fish" was captured by a camera meant to study the illusive effects of dark energy , which is the name scientists have given for whatever mysterious something is causing the universe to expand at an accelerating rate . The camera is used as part of the Dark Energy Survey, a six-year, international collaboration in which scientists have collected observations of hundreds of millions of galaxies, thousands of supernova and additional details about our cosmos that could help to fill in the picture of the nature of dark energy. And while researchers this past January revealed the initial result of this six-year survey, scientists continue to explore the possibilities of dark energy with DECam alongside instruments like the recently-launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. However, while the survey has lofty goals with its DECam data, the camera can also capture beautiful imagery like this cerulean wisp thousands of light-years away.

science.description: null The astronauts on the International Space Station will celebrate Thanksgiving with some nontraditional fare. Well, NASA astronaut Anil Menon will, anyway. In a video the agency released on Monday (Nov. 23), Menon showed off some of the plants he and his crewmates are growing in orbit and told us what's in store for the greens. "We need plants to survive as we set up our moon base , and as we go to Mars , we're going to have to grow our own nutrition. So that's what we're doing this Thanksgiving," Menon said in the 2.5-minute video. Astronauts deliver a Thanksgiving message from the International Space Station in November 2026. From left: NASA's Luke Delaney and Anil Menon, the Canadian Space Agency's Joshua Kutryk and NASA's Jessica Watkins. (Image credit: NASA) "I plan on using this [plant] with a tortilla and some pasta and some hot sauce to make my Thanksgiving meal," added Menon, who was wearing a chef's toque for the occasion. "And I'm grateful for you and for my family at home." He passed the microphone to fellow NASA astronaut Luke Delaney, who didn't talk about food but expressed gratitude to his family, crewmates and support network on Earth . Next up was NASA's Jessica Watkins, who gave us a rundown of the broader Thanksgiving menu in space. "Some of what we'll be eating here — we've got some roasted turkey, some mac and cheese, some mashed potatoes, and some candied yams," Watkins said, showing off the small bags containing each of those comestibles. "So, we should be in good shape." The Canadian Space Agency 's (CSA) Joshua Kutryk spoke next. He said he'll eat rice and the space-grown plants, which he'll consume raw "because it reminds me of Earth, which I miss." All four of the astronauts then wished us a happy Thanksgiving and did some zero-g flips and rolls, sending the space plants on a bit of a ride. Delaney, Kutryk and Watkins are members of SpaceX's Crew-13 mission, which arrived at the International Space Station (ISS) on Oct. 1 . There's a fourth Crew-13 astronaut as well — Sergey Teteryatnikov, of the Russian space agency Roscosmos . That quartet shares the ISS with Menon and cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina, who arrived in July aboard a Russian Soyuz spacecraft. Astronauts tend to get major holidays off on the ISS, and to celebrate them together. Doing so reinforces the already-strong bonds the crewmates share and helps them deal with the pain of being away from friends and family, which can be especially acute on holidays like Thanksgiving and Christmas. Kutryk is likely feeling especially emotional these days. On Tuesday, the CSA announced that Kutryk's wife had given birth to the couple's third child, a daughter. "Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our new little star into our lives," the couple said in a statement shared by the CSA. "We are very proud of our growing family and are looking forward to getting our little crew of five all reunited."

science.title: AI solved the hardest problem in maths – is there anything it can’t do?
science.description: Alzheimer’s disease, involving amyloid plaques in the brain, will be tough for AI to solve JUAN GAERTNER/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY The progress AI has made in mathematics this year is nothing short of extraordinary. In January, I was impressed to see relatively minor open problems tackled with the help of AI . Now, AI is being used to solve the hardest problems in maths . The obvious next question is, if AI can do this, is there anything it can’t do? That is the inference that the AI companies want us to make, but, in reality, the answer is much more nuanced. Read more Mathematicians are amazed by ‘holy grail’ proof of Riemann hypothesis We see this messaging in claims that AI can “solve X”, where X is any field of human endeavour you care to name. Biology is a big one. “Cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, mental illness – these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade,” said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei while promoting the company’s recent initial public offering . “I think one day maybe we can cure all disease with the help of AI,” said Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google DeepMind, last year , adding that this could be “within the next decade or so”. This phenomenon isn’t new: I call it “physicist brain”, after the propensity for physicists to wade into areas outside their expertise and declare simple solutions. More broadly, it is called Nobel disease , after the many Nobel prizewinners who have gone on to make, shall we say, less evidenced-backed claims. In general, there is a tendency to think that if an intelligent person is good at one thing, they are good at many other things that require intelligence. What is different now is that trillion-dollar companies and large swathes of the global economy now depend on this being true of artificial intelligence. Advertisement To be clear, I think we must now admit that AI is better at solving open mathematical problems than any human, and that this has happened faster than anyone ever expected. When I first saw the news in September that the Navier-Stokes problem had been solved by OpenAI , I felt stunned. We had entered a new world. With the announcement of the Riemann hypothesis proof this week, I felt sick and had to go and have a lie-down. These were intellectual Everests I have marvelled at since my teenage years, conquered by a machine far sooner than anyone expected. You may have read my recent piece forecasting the future in 2096 – an early draft had a line, later removed, about three Millennium Prize Problems being solved by AI in the 2030s. We’ve had two this year alone. But maths isn’t biology. Yes, we have seen advances like AlphaFold, Deepmind’s AI that can predict the structure of proteins , but this is biology at its most mathematical, a computational puzzle. True advances in biology and medicine require studying cells, animals and people, all of which can be frustratingly illogical and uncooperative. science.title: The defence tech revolution is changing how we innovate
science.description: Cpl Aaron J Stone/UK Ministry of Defence Only five years ago, defence technology start-ups had little choice but to wait for government funding to build and test their inventions – often in complex, multi-year programmes. No longer, however: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has prompted such a fast, furious response that military innovation timescales have shrunk dramatically. “Ukraine is becoming a real-world lab for military innovation, and it’s innovating at a pace greater than anything that we’ve seen previously,” says Ola Fashade, an air vice-marshal in the Royal Air Force and director of military digitalisation and the rapid AI delivery task force at the UK’s Ministry of Defence (MoD). “Agility and tempo of adaptation is critical. In a contested battlespace, technology that works well on day one, by day eight has become a little muted – and by day twelve it’s probably no longer relevant. And if you don’t adapt over that period, what you have is a very expensive and ineffective bag of steel.” Advertisement That raises the question of how significant this accelerated innovation could become. In September 2026, New Scientist CoLab, sponsored by BAE Systems, brought together leading thinkers and investors from industry, the military and academia to discuss the factors driving this innovation and the lessons that can be transferred to other industries. Staying alive The investment for this step change is coming both from the technology incubators based within military prime contractors – like the Launchpad incubator at BAE Systems – and from a host of venture capital (VC) companies worldwide. “The idea behind Launchpad is to forge an ecosystem that gets technology from defence start-ups into the front line quicker, or into spinouts, before they run out of money and die,” says David Ewing, head of technology commercialisation at BAE Systems. In addition, VC funding is seeing a raft of new multibillion-dollar military tech players, dubbed neoprimes, that complement the work of the primes on bigger-ticket battlespace items. The poster child for the neoprimes, says Samuel Burrell, a partner at the pan-European VC firm Expeditions Fund, is the nascent British air defence start-up Cambridge Aerospace, which reached a valuation of $3.4 billion with little but a convincing tech narrative: “They had no battlefield data, no product – just a compelling team and an idea on paper.” It wasn’t all talk: Cambridge Aerospace has begun delivering its Skyhammer air defence missile for taking out Shahed-type drones and cruise missiles. A solid-rocket-motor-powered ballistic missile interceptor, Starhammer, will ship in 2027. In the maritime battlespace, meanwhile, fast-scaling neoprime Kraken Technology Group of Hampshire, UK, has raised $175 million from various VC firms, valuing it at $1 billion, to further develop its uncrewed surface vessel and drone technologies for users including the MoD, NATO and the US Special Operations Command. science.title: Seeking Refuge on Resolution Island
science.description: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Seeking Refuge on Resolution… Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search In the late 1800s, wildlife conservationists in New Zealand were recognizing how predators such as stoats , brought to the country to control other nonnative animal populations, were becoming a threat to native birds. Naturalists at the time surmised that some of the nation’s islands could serve as sanctuaries where endemic species could persist, free from the voracious newcomers. Resolution Island, located in the Fiordland region along the rugged southwest edge of New Zealand’s South Island, was one of the first eyed for this purpose. Conservationist Thomas Henry Potts proposed in 1872 that the island could be a place where “wingless species, and birds of feeble powers of flight, might there find a refuge for some of their representatives.” So began an early systematic effort to protect kiwi, kākāpō , and other native birds on Resolution Island, the largest of the approximately 90 islands in Fiordland National Park . This image, acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on December 12, 2025, shows the island’s setting amid a landscape of steep-sided valleys carved by glaciers and now inundated by the ocean. The uninhabited island rises from sea level to the summit of Mount Clerke at 1,069 meters (3,507 feet). Its diverse habitats and vegetation communities range from bogs and wetlands near the coast to widespread podocarp forests at middle elevations to tussock grasslands in the subalpine and alpine areas. Offshore, the Taumoana (Five Fingers Peninsula) Marine Reserve protects estuarine and wave-exposed rocky reef habitats at the entrance to Dusky Sound, east of Five Fingers Peninsula. Farther into the sound, Pigeon Island was the onetime home of Richard Henry, who was named caretaker of Resolution Island after it was designated a reserve in 1891. In what some have called a “ landmark effort ,” Henry spent years transporting more than 700 birds, mostly kiwi and kākāpō, by rowboat to Resolution and other would-be island sanctuaries nearby. In 1900, however, people began spotting mustelids on Resolution. It turns out the island is within swimming distance for animals such as stoats. Henry was intent on trapping the interlopers but eventually abandoned the project and moved on to caretaking work on another island. The spirit of his efforts lives on, though. A Department of Conservation program started in 2008 aims to control stoat populations and bolster native species on Resolution. science.title: December full moon 2026: When, where and how to see the Cold Moon
science.description: null The December full moon reaches peak illumination at 8:28 p.m. EST on Dec. 23 (0128 GMT on Dec. 24) as the lunar disk shines opposite the sun in Earth's sky. It is often called the "Cold Moon" in reference to the frigid temperatures that prevail in the Northern Hemisphere around the time of its rising, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac . December's full moon will also occur close to perigee — the moon's closest point to Earth in its elliptical orbit — giving rise to a spectacular supermoon. A supermoon can appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than a full moon at its farthest point from Earth (also known as a micromoon).. According to the late, great astronomer Fred Espenak , the Cold Moon will be just 221,667 miles (356,740 kilometers) from Earth when it turns full, making it the closest supermoon of 2026! When to see the December full moon The full Cold Supermoon will make for a spectacular sight when it rises over the eastern horizon at sunset on Dec. 23, mere hours before reaching maximum illumination. Remember to use Time and Date's moonrise and moonset tracker for timings specific to your location. Earth's satellite may appear larger than normal while close to the horizon. This is partly because it is near perigee, when it appears subtly larger in the night sky, but also because of a phenomenon called the moon illusion, which tricks us into perceiving the moon to be bigger than it actually is while in the presence of foreground objects. A yellow full moon rises over Italy. (Image credit: Photo by Lorenzo Di Cola/NurPhoto via Getty Images) The moon may also adopt a striking golden or orange hue around moonrise and moonset. When the moon is low on the horizon, its light travels through more of Earth's atmopshere, scattering shorter, bluer wavelengths of light and allowing longer, redder wavelengths to reach our eyes. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 25, 1970: NASA's 'wingless' M2-F3 'lifting body' aircraft makes its 1st powered flight ahead of supersonic tests
science.description: null On Nov. 25, 1970, an experimental aircraft called the Northrop M2-F3 made its first powered flight. The M2-F3 aircraft was a heavyweight "lifting body" designed to test its ability to produce most of its lift through its fuselage instead of wings. It's commonly referred to as a "wingless" aircraft. After Air Force test pilot Bill Dana took the M2-F3 on three unpowered glide test flights, he did the first powered flight, too. Dana soared to an altitude of 45,000 feet during this flight, which lasted just over 6 minutes. He didn't break the sound barrier this time, but he did on later flights. The M2-F3 flew a total of 27 missions in its three-year flight history. Its top speed was 1.6 times the speed of sound, and its top altitude was 71,500 feet. NASA's M2-F3 lifting body drops from its carrier plane during a test flight in 1970. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered In the late 1960s and early 1970s, NASA was investigating lifting bodies as an approach to both new aircraft and what future spacecraft, and as its number suggests, the M2-F3 was not the first of its kind. In fact, the M2-F3 was a rebuilt version of its predecessor, the M2-F2 lifting body , after that vehicle crashed in a dry lake bed in California's Mojave Desert during an unpowered test flight. That crash (which appears in the opening of the TV show "The Six-Million-Dollar Man") led to upgrades for a better handling lifting body, NASA said. "When the M2-F2 was rebuilt and redesignated the M2-F3, it was modified with an additional third vertical fin – centered between the tip fins – to improve control characteristics," NASA wrote in an overview . Unpowered glide flights for the M2-F3 began in June 1970, but Dana's flight on Nov. 25 of that year was the first time the vehicle fired up its rocket engine to test its controls under powered flight. One vital upgrade on the vehicle was a set of reaction control thrusters to help maintain its orientation. "A reaction jet control system, similar to thrusters used on orbiting spacecraft, was also installed on the M2-F3 to obtain research data about their effectiveness for vehicle control," NASA wrote . "As the M2-F3’s portion of the lifting body program neared an end, it evaluated a rate command augmentation control system and a side-arm control stick similar to side-arm controllers now used on many modern aircraft." If you want, you can see the M2-F3 vehicle today. NASA donated it to the Smithsonian Institution. It is now hanging at the National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C. Want more space history? science.title: NASA Enhances Supplier Program, Announces Mentor-Protégé Agreement
science.description: NASA’s Office of Small Business Programs (OSBP) hosted a ceremonial Mentor-Protégé Agreement signing between The Boeing Company and GRACE Aerospace on Oct. 29, 2026, at the U.S. Space and Rocket Center in Huntsville, Alabama. Pictured in the front row, from left to right, are Pauline Sevigny, president and owner, GRACE Aerospace; Christian Diamond, Mentor-Protégé Program manager, The Boeing Company; and Dwight Deneal, assistant administrator, OSBP. Pictured in the back row, from left to right, are Danielle Barnes, small business specialist, OSBP; Grant Crawford, Logan Ojermark, Nikki Howard, and Sabrina Pearson, contracting officers, NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) stages team; Christen Edwards, lead, SLS stages team; Bradley Niese, NASA’s senior procurement executive, deputy chief acquisition officer, and assistant administrator, Office of Procurement; Chris Hall, program manager, OSBP; and Kristina Parmenter, procurement officer, NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center. Credit: Justin Fields, Light Rain Studio How NASA works with small businesses is evolving, and as a result, the agency is strengthening the domestic aerospace industrial base to support future exploration missions through its recently renamed Small Business Supplier Development Program. As part of the program, NASA announced its latest Mentor-Protégé Agreement, this one signed between The Boeing Company and GRACE Aerospace. NASA is streamlining the application process for the Small Business Supplier Development Program, as well as reducing administrative requirements, accelerating review and approval timelines, and enhancing incentives for prime contractor participation. These improvements are aimed at making supplier development more accessible, efficient, and closely aligned with NASA’s mission needs. “We have intentionally redesigned the program as a mission-focused tool for strengthening industrial base readiness and mission success,” said Dwight Deneal, assistant administrator, Office of Small Business Programs, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “By simplifying participation and focusing developmental assistance on the capabilities NASA needs most, we are helping build a stronger, more resilient supplier base that can support the agency’s highest-priority missions.” Under the new Mentor-Protégé Agreement, Boeing will provide structured assistance to help GRACE expand its capabilities as a supplier of mission-critical aerospace hardware. Boeing will fund the agreement, valued at nearly $500,000. “Boeing is proud to continue its longstanding relationship with NASA in support of its mission and the opportunities this agreement creates for Boeing, GRACE, and the broader aerospace industrial base,” said Christian Diamond, Mentor-Protégé Program manager and small business liaison officer for Boeing. “Through this partnership, Boeing looks forward to sharing our expertise to support the continued growth and long-term success of a small business while strengthening our supplier base.”

science.title: Seabird ‘spies’ could help spot ships that aren’t broadcasting their location
science.description: A northern gannet ( Morus bassanus ) tagged with biologging devices on its back and tail Steve Votier Audio from seabirds fitted with mini recording devices and GPS trackers has been used by researchers to show that marine life can record encounters with vessels that are otherwise difficult to track. Many large vessels are now legally required to carry automatic identification systems broadcasting their identity and location at regular intervals. Although this has allowed interactions between animals and fisheries to be studied at scale, there are enormous gaps in coverage. In fact, recent research suggests that three-quarters of industrial fishing vessels don’t use the technology, says Jonathan Rutter at the University of Oxford. This is partly because regulations on the types of vessels that are required to share data vary by country. Large satellite ‘blind spots’ also contribute to the problem, he says, and so does subterfuge for the purpose of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU). Advertisement Read more Most large fishing boats go untracked as ‘dark vessels’ Rutter says that being caught as bycatch in fishing is one of the greatest risks to seabird populations, but if fishing vessels are only tracked “with conventional methods, such footprints of risk may be strikingly incomplete”. The team analysed audio collected from devices attached to seven northern gannets ( Morus bassanus ) and found that one third of the audio detections couldn’t be matched with vessel tracking data – mostly off the UK coast. Overall, 12 per cent of the vessel detections made by the four critically endangered Balearic shearwaters ( Puffinus mauretanicus ) included in the study couldn’t be matched to public data. But given the high vessel density where they were – off the Catalan coast – the researchers estimated that up to 20 per cent of the vessels detected by the four birds weren’t broadcasting their identity. Tammy Davies at BirdLife International – a global partnership of non-governmental organisations – who wasn’t involved in the study, says the research could “give us a more complete picture of the risks seabirds face at sea” and “ultimately, this could contribute to better assessments of bycatch risk and help identify fisheries and areas where conservation measures are most needed”. Peter Ejbye-Ernst at the Netherlands Institute for the Study of Crime and Law Enforcement (NSCR), describes the study as “fascinating” from a green criminology point of view, too. A tagged northern gannet coming in to land in Wales Steve Votier “What this study is somewhat proposing is that we can also look outside of humans for witnesses too,” he says, which overcomes a key barrier in observing crime at sea.
